title: From Mount Nebo (Deuteronomy 34:1)
hook: Moses sees the whole land from the mountain
tomorrow: a kid asks about the rules. why does the answer start with a story?

segments.voice: Yesterday the last climb began: toward the summit, nearly there. Today an old man reaches a summit of his own, and stands very still.
screen: `NEARLY THERE.` → `AN OLD MAN ON A SUMMIT.`

segments.voice: The top level of a parking garage, late on a summer night. Noa and Owen climbed the stairs with two slushies, and Owen, laughing for the first time since his grandma's funeral, is pointing things out: the school, the water tower, her street, the park where they both learned to ride bikes. The whole town fits in one look. She leaves for college in two weeks, and from up here it looks finished, like a model of itself. She goes quiet. The Torah ends on a hilltop too. An old man climbs alone, and God shows him everything.
screen: `THE TOP OF THE GARAGE.` → `THE WHOLE TOWN IN ONE LOOK.` → `THE TORAH ENDS ON A HILLTOP.`

segments.voice: Deuteronomy's last chapter. Moses goes up from the plains of Moab to Mount Nebo, across from Jericho, and God shows him all the land, north to south, out to the far sea. Then the hard line, in the JPS translation: "I have caused thee to see it with thine eyes, but thou shalt not go over thither." He led a whole people through the wilderness toward this place, and he gets the view, not the walk. Some readers hear only grief in that. Others notice what the text adds a few verses on: "his eye was not dim." He sees clearly, all the way to the end. Rashi, the medieval commentator, says God showed him more than hills and valleys; he showed him what would happen there, the good days and the hard ones. Seeing it all means seeing the whole of something you won't finish. And here's a detail to tell someone tonight: the Torah says "no man knoweth of his sepulchre unto this day." No grave to visit. What's left of Moses is the teaching, and the people who walked on carrying it. A summit isn't the end of the road. It's the one place you can see the whole road, including the part that goes on without you.
screen: `UP FROM THE PLAINS OF MOAB.` · `YOU SEE IT; YOU DON'T GO OVER.` · `HIS EYE WAS NOT DIM.` · `NO ONE KNOWS HIS GRAVE.` · then, large: `SEE IT ALL.`

segments.voice: Go to the farthest view you can reach from where you are: a window, a doorway, a top step, a hallway with a long end. Let your eyes travel slowly from the nearest thing to the farthest, naming each one under your breath. When you reach the edge of what you can see, stop naming, and just look.
screen: `THE FARTHEST VIEW YOU CAN REACH.` · `NEAR TO FAR, NAMING.` · `AT THE EDGE, JUST LOOK.`

segments.voice: From Mount Nebo: the view Moses was given at the end. The whole land, seen clearly, and walked by the people after him.
Your line: see it all. The view first, then the people walk on with what you gave them. Two of fourteen, and the air is thinner up here.

howItsDone: Deuteronomy 34, Moses on Mount Nebo, is the Torah's last chapter; in synagogues it is read on Simchat Torah, when the yearly reading of the Torah ends and begins again at Genesis.

options: Moses got that view at the end too. Seeing it whole is a gift, even before you go.
Because looking back is the mistake. Moses kept his eyes only on the road ahead.

chat.meaning: On Nebo, Moses saw the whole land clearly, even the part others would walk into. A summit is where you can see it all.

Nebo.meaning: the mountain in Moab where Moses saw the land

Moab.meaning: the land east of the Jordan where Moses' journey ended

Jericho.meaning: a city across the Jordan, facing Nebo

Rashi.meaning: a medieval commentator on the Torah and Talmud
